observation: Bandura & Schunk (1981): children pursuing proximal subgoals in self-directed arithmetic learning showed faster progress, higher self-efficacy, and greater intrinsic interest than children given a distal goal (barely better than no goal) or no goal.
claim: Breaking a large goal into a sequence of near-term, session-scale subgoals causally improves both performance and motivation, especially for people with low prior confidence/interest.
mechanism: Proximal subgoals give frequent, unambiguous self-efficacy information that a distal goal cannot provide until the end.
population: children (grade-school), low prior interest/competence in domain

implications.text: FT-plan-breakdown should default to a sequence of near-term subgoals rather than a single distal goal, with visible frequent completion markers.

observation: Locke & Latham goal-setting meta-analytic literature: specific, difficult goals outperform vague 'do your best' goals in the large majority of comparisons, average performance gain ~17%, conditional on feedback and commitment.
claim: Vagueness itself is a performance cost independent of task decomposition; specific measurable steps outperform equally-sized vague ones.
mechanism: Specific goals reduce ambiguity about what counts as success, direct attention/effort, and enable self-monitoring against the goal.

implications.text: FT-plan-breakdown and FT-next-action should phrase each step as a specific, checkable outcome rather than a vague category.

observation: Cognitive-load research measuring at the subtask level finds meaningfully different load per subtask; a review of task-decomposition-for-reasoning names optimal sub-task granularity as an open, unsolved question, calling current practice arbitrary/heuristic.
claim: No evidence-backed universal 'right' size for a decomposed step exists; a fixed decomposition depth is an unjustified guess.
population: mixed (programming-education subgoal-labeling study; general cognitive-load-granularity review)

implications.text: FT-plan-breakdown should expose adjustable/adaptive granularity rather than a fixed step size.

observation: Buehler, Griffin & Ross found students' actual completion times substantially exceeded their own best-guess (and often worst-case) predictions; Kahneman/Lovallo framing identifies outside-view/reference-class estimation as the most reliable correction over inside-view reasoning.
claim: People systematically underestimate task duration by reasoning from the specific plan rather than from how long similar past tasks actually took; reference-class comparison is the evidenced fix.
mechanism: Inside-view planning anchors on a best-case causal scenario; comparing to actual outcomes of similar past tasks corrects the anchor by encoding unimagined obstacles.

implications.text: Time estimates in FT-plan-breakdown should be pulled from Sam's own logged history of similar past tasks, not generated as a fresh inside-view guess.

observation: Barkley-tradition and later meta-analytic time-perception research finds ADHD deficits concentrated in time reproduction (translating a felt interval into matched output) more than time estimation/perception; deficits span the lifespan and partially normalize on stimulant medication.
claim: The core ADHD time-blindness problem is using an internal sense of elapsed time to regulate ongoing action, not judging duration in the abstract, favoring external continuously-visible time cues during a task over upfront estimation exercises.
mechanism: Tracking elapsed time requires holding a temporal representation active against competing input, which is the resource ADHD executive dysfunction (behavioral inhibition/working memory) degrades.
population: adults, adolescents, and children with ADHD

implications.text: Prefer a continuously visible elapsed/remaining-time indicator during execution over a one-shot duration prediction.

observation: Norton, Mochon & Ariely (2012) found people valued self-assembled IKEA furniture, origami, and Lego builds comparably to expert-made work, but the effect disappeared when the object was destroyed or left incomplete.
claim: Self-generated artifacts are likely valued/owned more than equally-good handed-over artifacts, but only if the generation process reaches a completed state.
mechanism: Effort invested in successful completion is read as a competence signal and incorporated into liking for the object (effort-justification/ownership).

implications.text: Co-planning flow should ensure Sam always finishes constructing his plan rather than being handed a finished plan to merely approve; an abandoned co-planning session may confer none of the ownership benefit.

observation: SDT-informed ADHD commentary argues directive external control (tight schedules, close supervision, step-by-step instruction) thwarts the autonomy need ADHD motivation depends heavily on; separately, ADHD executive-function/coaching literature treats point-of-performance environmental scaffolding as more effective for initiation than teaching general planning skills.
claim: Being told the next action can help initiation but risks undermining autonomy/motivation if delivered as directive rather than as an offered, declinable suggestion; no study directly tests Riemann's specific accept/decline design.
mechanism: SDT distinguishes autonomy-supportive (informational, choice-preserving) from controlling (directive, pressuring) framing as having opposite motivational effects even for identical content.
context: mixed: clinical/coaching practice and theoretical review, not a single RCT

implications.text: FT-next-action should always be an offered, low-friction-declinable suggestion, never auto-advancing; log accept/decline/edit as an adaptivity signal.

observation: Longitudinal research found perceived autonomy support and autonomous motivation form a reciprocal, self-reinforcing loop over an academic year associated with positive affect and goal progress; collaborative goal-setting practice reports (e.g. family-driven autism-support planning) show higher goal-attainment when the person participates in setting the goal.
claim: The process of co-constructing a plan drives commitment/follow-through gains largely independent of whether the resulting plan is objectively better than an expert-handed one.
mechanism: Perceived choice/voice satisfies the SDT autonomy need directly; a plan reflecting the person's own input is easier to experience as 'mine'.
population: emerging adults (autonomy-support study, general population); autism-support population (goal-setting practice report)
context: longitudinal field study; clinical/service practice report

implications.text: Co-planning UI should visibly reflect Sam's own inputs/edits back into the generated plan rather than silently normalizing them away.

observation: Ariely & Wertenbroch (2002, Psychological Science) was retracted in September 2026 after Data Colada found data tampering (duplicated values, implausible correlations, a falsified analysis submitted to reviewers); a 2026 replication (Hyndman & Bisin) found deadline structure had a negligible effect on the original performance metrics.
claim: There is currently no credible experimental evidence that self-imposed or evenly-spaced deadlines reliably improve task performance relative to a single end deadline; the original numeric claims should not be relied on.
population: originally MIT executive-education students and undergraduates; replication used adults at a large US public university

implications.text: FT-commitment-capture should not be justified with claims that self-imposed deadlines are scientifically proven effective; the primary source for that claim is retracted for fraud.

observation: Rogers, Milkman & Volpp's meta-analysis of commitment-device RCTs reports a pooled effect around Hedges' g=0.68, but other work (e.g. a middle-school study) finds take-up doesn't necessarily change behavior, and commentary notes device adoption may signal pre-existing motivation rather than create it.
claim: Commitment devices have a moderate real effect on average, but heterogeneous and confounded by self-selection; a universally-offered device (not self-selected the way RCT participants self-select) may show a smaller true causal effect.
mechanism: Precommitment raises the cost of not following through via loss aversion on a forfeited stake, but only works if the person wants the underlying goal and trusts enforcement.
population: general adult (health-behavior RCTs); one middle-school study

implications.text: FT-commitment-capture should be opt-in for tasks Sam already wants to finish, not a pushed default nudge.

observation: A prospective study across 8 hospitals (N=7,688) found complication rates fell ~36% and death rates fell over 40% after introducing the WHO 19-item surgical safety checklist at three fixed checkpoints.
claim: A short, structured, externally-imposed checklist at fixed procedural checkpoints reliably catches errors of omission in high-stakes, multi-person, routine-but-critical procedures; this does not generalize to motivation-to-start problems for novel planning.
mechanism: Forces a brief explicit verbalized verification step that interrupts autopilot/skipped-step behavior under cognitive load and functions as team communication.
context: field, real hospitals, high-stakes team procedures

implications.text: Reserve checklist-style verification for repeatable multi-step procedures Sam has done before where the risk is a memory-slip under load, not for novel planning or motivation-to-start problems.

observation: Bellotti et al. (CHI 2004) found, contrary to 'people are bad at prioritizing' folk wisdom, that people have well-developed personal task-priority strategies; task-management failures were more about mismatched tools/reminding than an inherent inability to prioritize. Practitioner sources converge on vague task phrasing and unbounded list length as proximate causes of list abandonment.
claim: To-do list failure is usually poor task specification (vague items, no clear next physical action) and unmanaged length/visibility, not that list representations are inherently ineffective.
mechanism: A vague item requires an extra covert planning step before it's actionable; that decision cost disproportionately stalls people with ADHD task-initiation difficulty.
population: knowledge workers (Bellotti et al. field study)
context: field study of real task-management practice (email-centric, 2004 workplace)

implications.text: FT-next-action and FT-plan-breakdown should enforce concrete next-physical-action phrasing; list views should default to surfacing only the next 1-3 actionable items, not the full backlog.

observation: Dashboard-design practice literature and clinical/security alert-fatigue research converge on exception-based design (surfacing only deviations from an expected baseline) as the fix for monitoring-at-scale information overload, distinct from summarizing everything; industry practice for alerting systems has converged on differentiated batching (true exceptions in real time, everything else in a scheduled digest).
claim: For a monitoring objective, the right transform is diff/exception detection against an expected baseline, not compression/summarization of the full state, because compression reduces per-item cost but not the number of items reviewed while exception-filtering reduces the count itself.
mechanism: Compression preserves the count of items requiring a look; exception-filtering reduces the count, which is the actual attention-cost driver in a task defined by low expected information rate.
context: industry practice writeups + healthcare alert-fatigue systematic reviews

implications.text: FT-monitor-digest should be architected as a change-detection/diff engine surfacing only deltas from expected state, not a periodic LLM summary of everything watched; unchanged items should not appear at all.
